title: Variable Airflow Review
summary: Review a trigger-linked respiratory pattern using anatomy, observations and reversible-flow evidence. Training simulation—not clinical guidance.

patient.label: Case A — synthetic patient
patient.presentingComplaint: Episodic chest tightness and wheeze after exercise.
history: Symptoms vary from day to day and are more frequent during pollen season.
There is no smoking history, and symptoms improve after a reliever inhaler.

findings.label: Diffuse airway-wall change
findings.description: A diffuse illustrative wall-thickening pattern is visible along the central airway.

findings.label: Configured upper-lobe region
findings.description: A translucent region identifies the illustrative area used for spatial orientation.

differential.label: Asthma
differential.description: Variable trigger-linked airway narrowing with reversible airflow limitation.

differential.label: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
differential.description: Persistent airflow obstruction, usually with a relevant exposure history.

differential.label: Inducible laryngeal obstruction
differential.description: Intermittent upper-airway narrowing that can mimic lower-airway symptoms.

differential.label: Bronchiectasis
differential.description: Chronic airway dilatation, often associated with recurrent infection and sputum.

content.heading: Timing and triggers
content.body: Wheeze, cough and chest tightness vary over time, follow exercise and pollen exposure, and improve after a reliever.

content.alt: Illustration of a bronchiole leading to alveolar ducts and alveoli.
content.caption: Use the conducting-airway and gas-exchange landmarks during localisation.

content.title: Respiratory sound sample
content.transcript: Repeated musical, high-pitched expiratory sounds are audible.

content.title: Synthetic FEV1 comparison
content.summary: FEV1 rises from 2.45 L to 2.82 L after bronchodilator.

stages.title: Orient
stages.intro: Inspect the marked lobe and the configured airway findings before localising the relevant structure.

content.prompt: Inspect the marked right upper lobe, the configured region and the diffuse airway-wall change.
Localise the highlighted pathway from lobe to segment and airway structure.
content.explanation: The selected lobe and illustrative segment lead to a conducting small airway.

feedback.hint: Follow the visible hierarchy, then distinguish conducting airway from gas-exchange tissue.

stages.title: Observe
stages.intro: Select the observations that directly support a variable airflow pattern.

content.prompt: Which two observations carry the strongest diagnostic weight?

options.label: Symptoms vary with triggers and time

content.explanation: Trigger-linked variability and objective reversibility are the clearest supported pattern.

feedback.hint: Prioritise repeated pattern and measured change over one sound.

stages.title: Interpret
stages.intro: Separate functional evidence from supporting inflammatory context.

content.prompt: Classify each observation by its primary role.
content.explanation: Spirometry measures airflow change; the biomarkers add phenotype context.

content.statement: The before-and-after FEV1 values support reversible airflow limitation in this case.
content.explanation: The authored measurement increases after bronchodilator and supports reversibility.

stages.title: Conclude
stages.intro: Choose the hypothesis that best integrates the repeated pattern and measured airflow change.

content.prompt: Which hypothesis best fits the complete synthetic pattern?
content.explanation: Variable trigger-linked symptoms and reversible airflow limitation most strongly support asthma; wheeze and inflammatory markers remain supportive.

feedback.hint: Use the time pattern and spirometry together.

expertBenchmark.name: Authored respiratory-educator benchmark

rationales.foundation-explore: Inspecting the configured wall change and marked lobe establishes the spatial context without scoring it.
rationales.foundation-localise: The lobe and procedural segment lead to a bronchiole, the relevant conducting-airway choice.
rationales.foundation-key-observations: Variability and measured reversibility are stronger than a single sound or biomarker.
rationales.foundation-sort-evidence: Functional change and inflammatory context should be identified separately before synthesis.
rationales.foundation-reversibility: The authored FEV1 increase supports a reversible component.
rationales.foundation-best-diagnosis: The repeated trigger pattern and reversible flow change best support asthma among the authored alternatives.

path.label: Inspect before localising
path.detail: Use the marked lobe and configured wall finding to establish a spatial frame.

path.label: Prioritise pattern and function
path.detail: Give greatest weight to trigger-linked variability and measured bronchodilator response.

path.label: Use supporting evidence proportionately
path.detail: Treat wheeze and inflammatory markers as support rather than proof.

path.label: Compare the differential
path.detail: Choose the hypothesis that explains both the time course and reversible physiology.

evidenceWeights.note: The repeated trigger-linked course establishes variability.
The before-and-after measurement supplies objective reversible-flow evidence.
The illustrative wall change supports an airway process but is not diagnostic.
The markers add inflammatory context without determining the diagnosis.

expertBenchmark.diagnosisRationale: The authored combination of recurrent trigger-linked symptoms and improved FEV1 after bronchodilator is most coherent with asthma. The sound, biomarkers and configured wall change support an airway process but do not establish the diagnosis independently.

debrief.summary: The supported conclusion rests on symptom variability and reversible airflow limitation, with the spatial wall finding, wheeze and inflammatory markers used as supporting context.

keyEvidence.why: The trigger-linked recurrent course distinguishes variable from persistent obstruction.
The before-and-after FEV1 change provides the strongest functional support.
The configured finding connects exterior orientation to the conducting-airway localisation.
The expiratory sound supports airway narrowing but cannot determine the diagnosis alone.
